title: Ofsted’s menacing inspections are still disastrous. Schools should answer to the communities they serve | Simon Jenkins
summary:
For all the supposed improvements, inspectors still obsess over statistics and adjectives, but surely school success depends on teachers and parents

The government regulation of state schools by Ofsted in England is a fiasco. Following the 2023 suicide of the Reading headteacher Ruth Perry, after her school was downgraded from outstanding to inadequate, Ofsted appears to have referred to a dictionary. Single words were replaced by colour-coded report cards, which use a wider range of different adjectives to grade abstractions such as personal development and wellbeing, achievement and leadership. Never has the concept of “education” seemed so empty.

The reaction of the teaching profession to the new code has itself been devastating, as highlighted in a recent survey that showed more than half of headteachers in England polled after their schools were inspected under Ofsted’s new regime are now considering early retirement as a result of the experience. This sense of misery was also illustrated in a poll conducted by the National Education Union one year on from the introduction of the new framework, with 65% saying it is the same as or worse than before.

Simon Jenkins is a Guardian columnist

full_text:
The government regulation of state schools by Ofsted in England is a fiasco. Following the 2023 suicide of the Reading headteacher Ruth Perry, after her school was downgraded from outstanding to inadequate, Ofsted appears to have referred to a dictionary. Single words were replaced by colour-coded report cards, which use a wider range of different adjectives to grade abstractions such as personal development and wellbeing, achievement and leadership. Never has the concept of “education” seemed so empty.

The reaction of the teaching profession to the new code has itself been devastating, as highlighted in a recent survey that showed more than half of headteachers in England polled after their schools were inspected under Ofsted’s new regime are now considering early retirement as a result of the experience. This sense of misery was also illustrated in a poll conducted by the National Education Union one year on from the introduction of the new framework, with 65% saying it is the same as or worse than before.

It is no wonder that the leader of the National Association of Head Teachers, Paul Whiteman, has called for an immediate halt to Ofsted’s visits. “The clear theme emerging across all the feedback we have received is that this Ofsted framework is even more stressful than the one that preceded it,” he said. “It poses a real and present danger to the well-being and mental health of school leaders and teachers, possibly even a risk to life.” Even the new education secretary, Lucy Powell, has said she takes the reaction to the inspections “incredibly seriously” and said she wanted to see a system that was “more supportive” to staff. We have yet to see what that means.

Schools used to be local institutions that belonged to the community. Bringing state-maintained schools under central government control in England and Wales began in 1988 with Thatcher’s national curriculum reforms. In 1992, John Major created Ofsted to enforce it. He also began a national league table of secondary schools, which were to be judged by their exam results. It is hardly surprising that the whole dynamic of secondary education became “to teach the exam”. Sports, art, music were shamelessly sidelined.

By the time of Tony Blair, the resulting avalanche of Whitehall regulations was said by a teacher friend to fill a wheelbarrow every school term. Vocational and technical education were demoted in favour of academic and university-oriented subjects. The nation’s performance in the international Pisa league tables became as competitive as the Olympic Games.

Now, Ofsted inspectors descend on schools, usually once in four years, with usually just 24 hours’ notice. They are armed not with advice or money but with exam statistics and adjectives. They have reduced the teaching profession to a production line.

The trauma experienced by staff has been an inevitable consequence. Perry’s sister says she has been contacted by 12 other heads saying they too have felt suicidal after glib dismissals of their work. How could such a brief inspection take account of considerations as important as a child’s health, the local job requirements and tutoring resources? An inspector merely needed to sniff the air, decide “not good enough” and stroll back to Whitehall. Would we judge our doctors, lawyers or bankers that way?

The naivety of the inspection regime is a classic of overcentralised government, of the relentless search for standardisation. I can find no evidence that relates a pupil’s or a school’s exam results to an individual’s wealth or happiness in later life. They are measuring for measuring’s sake.

The one great fault of comprehensive education in Britain from the 1960s onwards was its devoting so much of the secondary syllabus to academic subjects. Powell has already shown herself open to reforming this. She has banned GCSE preparation from the first two years of secondary school, and is determined to end the denial of vocational education for those who fail maths GCSE. Her proposal to teach subjects such as health and social care is welcome. So too is her enthusiasm for oracy and verbal confidence. If Powell means what she has said, she must put an end to Michael Gove’s generation of ministers and their obsession with academic league tables and to preparing pupils for university.

Possibly Britain’s currently most disgraceful statistic is that since the outbreak of Covid about 20% of children in England in year 9 – their mid-teens – are “persistently absent” from school. We need look no further for the cause of the current Neets crisis. The failure is glaring.

The success of a school, primary or secondary, is largely a function of its relationship with its local area. It depends on the reputation of its staff and their collaboration with parents. When schools were locally owned and run prior to Thatcher’s nationalisation these relationships were built into their governance. A school’s success was a feature of local pride. Of course this meant some worked better than others. But I find it significant that the UK was recently rated only the 16th “happiest country” in Europe. In part I sense it reflects its distant and heavily centralised public sector.

Nobody needs Ofsted. Andy Burnham should move to devolve schools to the communities they serve and on which they should in future depend. Inspecting the professional quality of their work should be a local matter. We need only to look abroad to see that this works.

title: With free-tuition promises, some colleges try to untangle confusion over what they cost
summary:
MIDDLEBURY, Vt. — Stately buildings of Vermont limestone surround meticulously tended lawns at the edge of a New England village that looks like it’s the setting for a Hallmark Christmas movie. There’s a golf course on this campus. The student-faculty ratio is an exclusive 9-to-1. And an undergraduate tour guide is telling visiting prospective applicants […]

The post With free-tuition promises, some colleges try to untangle confusion over what they cost appeared first on The Hechinger Report.
full_text:
MIDDLEBURY, Vt. — Stately buildings of Vermont limestone surround meticulously tended lawns at the edge of a New England village that looks like it’s the setting for a Hallmark Christmas movie.

There’s a golf course on this campus. The student-faculty ratio is an exclusive 9-to-1. And an undergraduate tour guide is telling visiting prospective applicants about a classmate who spent a semester learning how to forage in Malaysia.

Middlebury College looks and sounds … expensive. But like other universities and colleges, it’s working hard to persuade people that it’s not.

Middlebury has announced that, starting next year, students from families with annual household incomes up to $175,000 can enroll tuition-free. It becomes the latest of a growing number of schools to make this kind of promise, including Princeton (for most families earning up to $250,000, with typical assets), the University of Chicago ($250,000), MIT ($200,000), Harvard ($200,000), Swarthmore ($200,000) and Davidson ($175,000).

These may seem like generous expansions of financial aid; after all, $175,000 is more than double the nation’s median household income. But while it’s true that few additional families will benefit — 35 to 50 in the incoming class at Middlebury, which typically enrolls about 630 new students per year, the college says — most people in those earnings categories already attend without having to pay tuition.

Related: Interested in innovations in higher education? Subscribe to our free biweekly higher education newsletter.

When families see these pronouncements, they think, “ ‘Oh, wow, the college is cutting the price.’ And that’s almost a perfect example of the misperceptions of the pricing system,” said Phillip Levine, an economist at Wellesley College who studies higher education finance and is the author of the book “Hidden Tuition: An Insider’s Guide to College Pricing and Financial Aid.”

In fact, said Levine, whose research bears this out, at most of the institutions making these tuition-free guarantees, “the college was already free for almost all those kids.”

The real purpose of what Middlebury and other schools are doing, he and other experts say, is to solve a problem that has soured many Americans on higher education: how frustratingly hard it is to figure out what college will cost.

“Let’s make it as non-complicated as possible,” said Ian Baucom, president at Middlebury: “If your family income is $175,000 or less, at Middlebury, you don’t pay tuition.” What the school is doing, he said, is trying to “just [be] really clear and get that out of the way, and then let the students decide.”

Most of the growing number of income-based tuition plans take effect next year, as at Middlebury, or began for students who enrolled this fall.

That’s not coincidental. Many of these schools have reached or surpassed a listed price of attendance of $100,000 a year; at Middlebury, it’s $97,386. And public confusion about how much they actually cost after discounts and financial aid is helping drive a near-record-low confidence in higher education that threatens to exacerbate enrollment and revenue challenges.

Nearly 70 percent of students and parents think the financial aid process is partly or completely confusing, according to a separate survey by the Strada Education Foundation.

Most Americans also think that colleges are overpriced, with nearly two-thirds saying four-year institutions are unaffordable, a Gallup survey found; among parents who don’t want their children to go to a four-year college, it found, the biggest reason was the cost.

Related: Some colleges aim financial aid at a declining market: Students in the middle class

Yet more than three-quarters of adults without college degrees couldn’t correctly estimate the price of a public four-year institution within $5,000, another survey, by Gallup and the Lumina Foundation, showed. (Lumina and Strada are among the funders of The Hechinger Report, which produced this story.)

A culprit for this is colleges’ own increasingly self-destructive policy of advertising a high list price that almost no one pays, then giving discounts. It’s a strategy that has evolved from a time when the price was intended to signal value and the discounts — which the colleges call “scholarships” — to entice the most desirable prospective students to enroll.

So much has that spiraled that, at 445 colleges and universities of all kinds, not a single student now pays the advertised price, according to a Hechinger Report analysis of federal data. At private, nonprofit four-year universities and colleges, fewer than 1 in 5 families pay that amount, an analysis of federal data shows.

Yet consumers appear fixated on that listed “sticker” price.

Nearly 80 percent of families considering sending a student to college eliminated a school from consideration based on the price, a survey by the student loan company Sallie Mae found.

It’s often low-income students, and young people whose parents didn’t go to college, who find the price and the process of financial aid hardest to decipher, admissions officials say.

“The most important problem, I would argue, in college pricing today is the lack of transparency,” said Levine, who said that even he had trouble figuring out the prices when he sent his sons to college, despite his Ph.D. in economics.

“If you’re going to charge people different amounts of money, you have to provide them with some indication of what that’s going to be. Or how are they supposed to make good financial decisions? And for the most part, we don’t do a very good job of accomplishing that goal,” Levine said.

One reason is that colleges often don’t give families a final price until after a student is accepted and submits financial documents.

Related: As college graduates fret over finding jobs, a record shortage of workers is projected

“I mean, you’re waiting till the end to see how it all shakes out, and you won’t know until, really, you have your FAFSA filled out,” said Liz Mark, a mother from Wisconsin, referring to the free application for federal student aid.

Mark, who was visiting Middlebury with her high school junior, Charlotte, compared it to the pricing system for medical care.

“It’s a little bit like going to the doctor, right? You don’t know exactly how much a procedure is going to cost until you get all of that information and get your pre-approvals,” she said.

Another parent touring Middlebury, Mark Doughty, said he was lucky to have a friend who works in higher education, and who helped him better understand the process.

“The price on the menu is not necessarily what you pay,” Doughty said he learned.

“If you don’t have some guide through the system, then you could walk in and pay way more than you have to,” said Doughty, of Massachusetts, who already has a son at Middlebury and a daughter considering applying there.

Free-tuition promises based on family income are at least “creating a very clear ceiling,” he said.

There are two even newer reasons to do this than the principal one of making prices more transparent, said Nicole Curvin, dean of admissions and vice president of strategic enrollment at Middlebury: general anxiety about the cost of living and a fast-changing labor market.

“The economy is all over the place. Undergraduates are concerned about their employment opportunities. They are concerned about everything from AI to world dysfunction,” Curvin said. “Affordability is the top question that every family is asking us, and we have to be willing to address that.”

Related: College admissions offices take on a new role: Coaxing accepted students to show up

Other colleges are also looking for ways to make their prices more transparent.

A few are simply lowering them, including Prescott College in Arizona, the University of Tulsa and Concordia University, St. Paul in Minnesota.

The University of Pennsylvania, which already makes tuition free for students from families earning $200,000 a year or less, just debuted a calculator that can tell families — before they apply — how much going to the university will cost them. “Penn is more affordable than most people realize,” blares the heading at the top of the calculator web page.

“Higher ed in general is trying to respond to some of those concerns, some of those questions” about what college really costs, said Mariana Valdes-Fauli, the university’s associate vice president of student registration and financial services. “This really just kind of opens our door to our financial aid process and what we consider and what we don’t, to allow all kinds of students to see that Penn is a real option.”

It’s not a perfect solution. Free tuition guarantees don’t cover room, board, books, transportation or other expenses — $24,462 a year at Middlebury — though other financial aid is often available for those.

Colleges with fewer resources are offering promises of free tuition to more limited audiences.

Earlham College is making tuition free for students from families earning $100,000 a year or less who live in its home state of Indiana. First-year students in New Hampshire whose families earn $100,000 or less will be eligible for free tuition to that state’s public universities and colleges.

At North Carolina’s private Wake Forest University, starting this fall, in-state students from families earning $200,000 or less pay no tuition. Marist University in New York is capping tuition, room and board at $32,000 a year starting next fall for new students from that state whose families have incomes of $200,000 or less.

The common motivation, said Baucom, the Middlebury president, is the realization that consumers “are broadly aware that there is financial aid, but often it’s just difficult to figure out, ‘How does it work? How do I get access to it?’ ”

The stakes are higher than just whether someone might apply to Middlebury, and who gets to attend there, he said.

“The social contract of American life depends upon the idea that everyone can come into the fullness of what it means to live and think and study and work here. And that’s fracturing,” Baucom said.

The sight of the idyllic campus outside the window of his office, “might convey [that] this is not for your family,” he acknowledged. “And I just want to be as simple and clear as possible: We want every family, and families of all sorts.”

*Correction: This story has been corrected to clarify what is included in Marist University’s policy capping tuition, room and board.

Contact writer Jon Marcus at 212-678-7556, jmarcus@hechingerreport.org or jpm.82 on Signal.

This story about the cost of college was produced by The Hechinger Report, a nonprofit, independent news organization focused on inequality and innovation in education. Sign up for our higher education newsletter.

title: One City’s Game Plan to Retain International Students
summary:
One City’s Game Plan to Retain International Students Johanna Alonso Fri, 11/13/2026 - 03:00 AM As the Trump administration narrows pathways for international students to work in the U.S., more than 100 Philadelphia-area higher education, nonprofit and business leaders gathered to discuss how to keep them in the city. Byline(s) Johanna Alonso One City’s Game Plan to Retain International Students
Johanna Alonso Fri, 11/13/2026 - 03:00 AM

As the Trump administration narrows pathways for international students to work in the U.S., more than 100 Philadelphia-area higher education, nonprofit and business leaders gathered to discuss how to keep them in the city.

Byline(s)
Johanna Alonso
full_text:
PHILADELPHIA—Every year, the greater Philadelphia area sees about 23,000 international students studying at its scores of colleges and universities. Yet the number who remain in the city to work after graduation constitutes just a sliver of that. In 2023, of the city’s 1,333 international graduates working on optional practical training, the postgraduation work program for international students, just a third, or 421, stayed in the region to do so, according to research conducted by the Economic League of Greater Philadelphia and presented this week at the inaugural Philadelphia: A Global Education Hub conference.

The two-day event at Temple University brought together the city’s higher education, business and nonprofit sectors to discuss not just how to recruit more international students, but also how to convince them to stay in the city after they graduate. According to data presented at the conference by Anuj Gupta, president and CEO of the Welcoming Center, a Philadelphia nonprofit focused on workforce development for immigrants, foreign-born Philadelphians are a major boon to the city’s economy; they frequently open small businesses, and foreign-born employers throughout the state are hiring more of their fellow Pennsylvanians. Research also shows that a higher number of individuals working on STEM optional practical training, which allows graduates of U.S. STEM programs to stay and work for three years, leads to an increase in innovation and new start-ups in the cities where they live.

But the Philadelphia coalition’s goals are virtually antithetical to the goals of the Trump administration, which has claimed that international students who stay to work in the U.S. take jobs from domestic graduates. The Department of Homeland Security is currently seeking to impose a $70,000 fee on colleges for every student who applies for OPT, a policy change that some in higher education say would all but end the program.

International House Philadelphia, a nonprofit that supports international students in the region, has been working on improving international student recruitment and retention in the area since before Trump’s second term, said Bill Keyes, IHP’s executive director, in an interview before the conference.

The effort is a part of a larger effort, called the PA Global Talent Collaborative, to create conditions to attract more international talent to the commonwealth at large.

While the event touched on federal changes to work authorization, that wasn’t its main focus; after all, some speakers noted that the Trump administration’s previous efforts to decrease the number of foreign workers in the U.S., such as attaching a $100,000 to H-1B visas, haven’t yet been successful.

“This is not a time to raise our hands and recoil,” said Charity Alinda, director of international student and scholar advising at Bryn Mawr College, during a panel about federal changes. “It’s time to double down because, when things get better, you don’t want to get left behind in the process.”

Attendees focused instead on how to make Philadelphia a place where international students not only want to come for college but also stay after graduation. They discussed everything from attracting companies that international students want to work for to making the students’ transition into the country easier.

Tasks like setting up a bank account or finding housing might seem small, and even when challenging, they are not likely to cause a student to leave their institution, Yuhong He, director of integration, community engagement and marketing at International Student and Scholar Services at the University of Pennsylvania, said at a roundtable discussion about state and local policy. But repeated frustrations could leave the student with a negative impression of Philadelphia, which might dissuade them from staying in the city—or recommending it to their friends back home.

“This is where we can really make significant changes for people’s lives,” said Keyes. For example, a college could educate incoming international students on unfamiliar aspects of American life, like negotiating health-care bills. “An international student who comes here from a background where you pay what the sticker price is … wouldn’t know that you could do that,” he said. “That would seem nuts.”

Speakers also highlighted the importance of creating a sense of belonging for international students in Philadelphia. One session discussed how connecting students with immigrant communities in the city can help them feel more welcome, while another pitched volunteerism around the city as one avenue for students to form a deeper connection with the surrounding community.

Still, even volunteering can be more complicated for international students than it is for domestic students. Some programs, like Big Brothers Big Sisters of America, require volunteers to have a Social Security number. Others may not be easily accessible by public transit, and the majority of international students do not own cars.

Visa issues can also get in the way; if the volunteer opportunity is too similar to the student’s course of study, DHS may consider it an unapproved unpaid internship, noted one attendee who asked not to be named.

Employment Hurdles

Job opportunities remain a major hurdle for international graduates. Philadelphia’s economy is historically based around “eds and meds”—higher education and health care—with fewer opportunities for office-based jobs in fields like finance. The city has been working in recent years to attract more businesses, but it’s not keeping pace with the growing talent pool. Speakers stressed that luring more opportunity to the city was key to getting international talent to stay.

Working in the city as an international student can be difficult, panelists said. Even when companies don’t have to sponsor an applicant because they’ve been authorized for OPT, some won’t hire international students due to misconceptions that doing so would be unlawful, said Kristen Gallo, executive director for career services at Temple University.

“It’s very difficult as one university. I don’t know what [businesses] hear from their own leadership,” she said. “It does tend to be just a lack of information, a lack of understanding, that they’ve rolled into their own organizational policy or practices.”

Andrea Hearn, director of human resources at the Children’s Crisis Treatment Center, a nonprofit that provides behavioral health services to children, noted that the center has made a concerted effort to be more welcoming to international workers, including by providing English-language training and assisting employees in earning clinical licenses. As a nonprofit, they’re also exempt from the cap on H-1B visas.

The effort has paid off: The company now employs over 30 foreign-born workers, who have had great retention rates and created a strong referral pipeline for other members of their communities, Hearn said.

In the session on local policy, Keyes also pointed at laws that make working in the state more difficult for international students, such as a requirement that Pharm.D. students must have a Social Security number to do their internships.

Keyes hopes to take the discussions from the conference and develop a report to inform steps the city can take to attract and retain more international students.

“We’re really trying to put on a pedestal what we’re talking about at the conference: what international students and scholars contribute to our region, why we need to have them here and how we can best support them,” he said.

title: ‘AI Slop’ Papers Published Under Prominent Academics’ Names
summary:
‘AI Slop’ Papers Published Under Prominent Academics’ Names Susan H. Greenberg Fri, 11/13/2026 - 03:00 AM High-profile researchers were listed among authors at little-known titles, sparking concern that Ph.D. students could be tempted to submit their work there, too. Byline(s) Seher Asaf for Times Higher Education ‘AI Slop’ Papers Published Under Prominent Academics’ Names
Susan H. Greenberg Fri, 11/13/2026 - 03:00 AM

High-profile researchers were listed among authors at little-known titles, sparking concern that Ph.D. students could be tempted to submit their work there, too.

Byline(s)
Seher Asaf for Times Higher Education
full_text:
A group of little-known academic journals has been publishing “AI slop” papers under the names of professors who did not write them, sparking concerns that academics’ identities are being misused, an investigation has found.

Alan Said, professor of computer science at the University of Gothenburg, came across the journals after he received a notification from Google Scholar about a paper published under his name in the American International Journal of Research and Innovation (AIJRI).

The article, titled “Intelligence Systems Supporting Sustainable Global Development,” was loosely related to his research on artificial intelligence and sustainability, but he did not write the paper.

“It wouldn’t be surprising if I wrote a paper on something around this topic, but just looking at this paper and looking at the citations in the paper, it looks AI-generated. It has no content, it’s like slop,” he said.

He reported the incident to the journal’s domain registrar, who told him that the article had been removed. But the paper remained online and his name had been replaced with that of another individual. Screenshots shared with THE show that two days later the author had changed again, leaving three versions of the same paper attributed to different authors. AIJRI/Getty Images montage

Said also came across the American Journal of Advanced Multidisciplinary Research and Innovation (AJAMRI) and the American Journal For Multidisciplinary Research (AJFMR)—two other journals using similar graphics, with the same editor in chief and board members. The former has published dozens of papers attributed to high-profile academics, including Stanford computer scientists Fei-Fei Li and Christopher Manning and Berkeley professors Michael I. Jordan and Stuart Russell.

All three domain names were registered in 2026, but the websites show archives of papers supposedly published several years earlier. The journals all describe themselves as “peer-reviewed, open access and multidisciplinary.” The websites also advertise publication fees. AIJRI and AJAMRI said they charge $200 for papers written by five or more non-Indian authors, while the AJFMR charges $80 for one to four authors or $10 for five or more authors.

“They all seem to be the same type of operation. Very shallowly written or generated,” Said said. “I’m concerned, because if a new Ph.D. student were to see my name in this journal, they might think it’s OK to submit there, too, and I would really not want that to happen.”

Several academics listed in the journals have confirmed that they did not write the articles or consent to their names appearing there.

Jure Leskovec, professor of computer science at Stanford University, is among those named as an author in the journal. “I can confirm that I did not write this paper, was not involved in its submission and did not authorize the use of my name. I was also unaware of its existence until [THE’s] email. This is quite concerning,” he said.

All three journals identify their editor in chief as Denish Brown and have a WhatsApp number with a U.S. area code. Times Higher Education contacted the journals but did not receive a response before publication.

The journals also list dozens of editorial board members affiliated with mostly Indian higher education institutions.

One of them, Kanakaraju Manupati, a postdoctoral fellow at Virginia Commonwealth University, told THE that he had not agreed to serve on the boards. “I was not aware of the existence of this journal and was not associated with it. I just checked the journal website, surprised to see my name on the editorial board,” he said.

THE has contacted others on the editorial board.

title: ‘The Worst I’ve Ever Seen It’
summary:
‘The Worst I’ve Ever Seen It’ Sara Brady Fri, 11/13/2026 - 03:00 AM The world that students are facing is meaningfully different now than it was in the last couple of crises. Byline(s) Matt Reed ‘The Worst I’ve Ever Seen It’
Sara Brady Fri, 11/13/2026 - 03:00 AM

The world that students are facing is meaningfully different now than it was in the last couple of crises.

Byline(s)
Matt Reed
full_text:
A trusted colleague mentioned in a meeting recently that she has never seen more students more stressed out than she sees now. She’s not the type who’s prone to drama, so when she declared student stress the worst she’s ever seen, I took notice.

From the outside, you might think that the farther away we get from the worst of the pandemic, the closer we’d get to normal. But in terms of student perceptions, that doesn’t seem to be true.

The world that students are facing is meaningfully different now than it was in the last couple of crises. When the economy’s wheels came off in 2008, people flocked to campus; enrollments hit historic peaks around 2009–10 as the opportunity cost of education hit a new low. The rest of the economy was contracting hard, but campuses were lively. (Online classes were also a much smaller proportion of offerings then.) Campuses felt like oases from the recession, and there was a general sense among students that as bad as things were, they would recover.

When the pandemic hit in 2020, anxiety spiked as well, but much of it was invisible from a campus perspective. And even then, at least for a while, there seemed to be a belief that this too would pass. The immediate moment had a surreal feeling to it, for obvious reasons, but students still had a sense that there would be opportunities waiting for them when they graduated.

Over the last year or so, a couple of subtler changes set in. Students felt them quickly.

One was the spike in gas prices immediately after the start of the Iran war. It jumped about $1.50 a gallon or so in the early spring, and is still about $1.30 more than it was a year ago. My county’s public transit system is pretty modest; most students drive to campus and jobs. When you’re struggling to pay tuition and keep yourself fed, an abrupt and sustained double-digit-percentage increase in the cost of driving hits pretty hard. Had the spike lasted a few weeks, it would have been annoying. Lasting most of the year, it has become a real obstacle for people living paycheck to paycheck. (I also suspect it’s part of what powered the blue wave in the midterm election. Voters blame incumbents for expensive gas.)

The other is AI and its effect on the entry-level job market. Unless you’re in health care or one of a few skilled trades—the latter being boosted by data centers—it’s not entirely clear which career fields offer a real future anymore. It’s easier to give in to what Kyla Scanlon sometimes calls financial nihilism. It’s one thing to sacrifice for an education with a plausible and appealing payoff; it’s quite another to sacrifice for an education reflecting a world already on its way out.

The combination of two, from the perspective of someone just starting out, can be demotivating. Education becomes both harder to access and less obviously a route to the middle class. Online classes help with the transportation piece, but students who take a lot of them can feel (and be) isolated, with negative effects both for retention/completion and learning. That combination of isolation and felt pointlessness can lead to all manner of anxiety.

That’s fundamentally different from the last couple of crises. As different as the great recession and the pandemic were from each other, neither seemed to threaten the long-term economy. They felt like intense storms that would pass; at some point, “normal” would return. AI threatens to hollow out better-paying jobs, preventing the previous normal from ever returning. Folks who are already established in their careers may be able to ride out the clock, but young people trying to break in are facing an undefinable future. Young adulthood is a stressful time anyway, as people try to figure out who they are and what their place in the world will be. Make the world less legible, and the stress is that much worse.

To the extent that we can, we owe it to students to help build the skills likely to matter in any particular economy. And we owe them whatever clarity we can offer about the world they’ll inhabit longer than we will.

title: COVID-19 school disruptions still impacting students today, learning loss report finds
summary: A new report says Canadian students are still feeling the impact of the COVID pandemic's massive upset to their schooling, with declining achievement — particularly in math — and a discrepancy between standardized test scores and the grades kids receive in class.
full_text:
Canadian students are still recovering from the pandemic's massive upset to their schooling, with evidence of declining achievement — particularly in math — across jurisdictions, according to a new report.

The report, released Thursday by the Royal Society of Canada, the Canadian Commission for UNESCO and the University of Ottawa, also notes a discrepancy between standardized test scores and the grades kids receive in class

It takes an in-depth look at pandemic learning loss and recovery by examining students' academic results in language arts and mathematics before, during and after COVID-19. Nearly three dozen researchers parsed data from Canadian ministries of education, save Manitoba and Nunavut, which didn't participate.

They analyzed the results of standardized tests, as well as teacher-assigned grades across different grades and — depending on the jurisdiction — considered factors like gender and location (for instance, rural and remote communities versus urban ones).

The pandemic is "going to influence learning for the next few decades and that's not exaggeration," said Tracy Vaillancourt, chair of the report and a professor of education at the University of Ottawa.

"These effects are going to be felt for generations to come."

The report is divided by studies of individual provinces and territories, with the findings differing across regions, student populations and grades, said Vaillancourt, who's also the Canada Research Chair in youth mental health and violence prevention.

That's not surprising given the varying local contexts of each jurisdiction, including how each assesses learning, coupled with the patchwork of pandemic responses taken: from how long each closed schools and opted for remote learning to physical distancing in classrooms to recovery efforts implemented afterwards.

Yet across each of the report's individual provincial and territorial studies, there are some broader commonalities, she said:

Declines in standardized test results, notably in math. In particular, an emerging gender gap with declining math achievement for girls in several regions and girls' math scores not recovering as quickly as boys have.

A greater impact on younger students, who saw the very building blocks of their foundational knowledge affected — like learning what numbers mean or how to read — versus older students with the basics already established.

A discrepancy between achievement measured by standardized tests, where scores have fallen, versus teacher-administered grades, which rose.

Grade inflation is real, says Vaillancourt, but "this isn't a knock on teachers at all. They were in a really difficult situation" given the high stress of that time.

Teacher grades also tend to incorporate learning progress, she said. High-stakes tests capture a snapshot of student knowledge during one window of time.

During the pandemic, many school systems dropped exams (which never returned in some cases) and asked teachers to weigh assignments differently. Some teachers were directed to reduce content being covered amid the glut of obstacles facing educators and learners alike, ranging from inconsistent or unavailable internet to quarantines to toggling between in-person and online learning.

Researchers also found the pandemic had mixed impacts on reading and writing scores, and that students in some rural, remote and northern communities saw greater declines in overall achievement — and are taking longer to recover — than urban peers.

Taking action

The report lands more than three years after COVID-19 was downgraded from global emergency status. Its authors make several recommendations to governments, starting with support for standardized testing in order to establish reliable, comparable benchmarks of student achievement over time.

In a time of emergency, "we've got to be compassionate about how kids are faring … but we should also, if possible, monitor what's going on," Vaillancourt said.

"Putting our head in the sand doesn't do anything; it doesn't identify who's most vulnerable [and] how to remedy that vulnerability."

Another recommendation urges the prioritization of evidence-based methods to tackle learning loss — paying particular attention to the most disadvantaged students — and the continual evaluation of whether these initiatives are working.

COVID worsened existing concerns

The report's findings and recommendations weren't a surprise, since teachers have voiced similar concerns for years, says Clint Johnston, president of the Canadian Teachers' Federation, which represents more than 390,000 teachers and education workers.

"What I see is an exacerbation of a context that honestly already exists in an under-resourced system. We've got children who are falling a bit behind, they're not getting the support they need," he said from Toronto.

"It's not surprising that when there was an interruption, there'd be an impact."

Addressing gaps requires investment, Johnston said, "and right now it essentially seems like we're being asked to make up those gaps — to do more with the same amount — which isn't really feasible."

Montreal parent Katherine Korakakis, whose two kids required tutoring during and after the pandemic, praised the report for validating what parents have long worried about.

"We knew that the pandemic disrupted our children's education, but the questions always were, how significant were those disruptions?"

Korakakis, who's president of Quebec's English Parents' Committee Association, backs the report's call to identify students with learning gaps, implement initiatives supporting them and provide continued monitoring.

"Parents need a clear, set plan with meaningful actions and measurable progress," she said.

A final recommendation urges emergency preparedness planners to recognize how detrimental prolonged school closures have been, including affecting kids' broader well-being. Schools are typically where youngsters find social connection, a safe space and myriad supports, including food programs and mental health services.

During emergencies, provided it is safe to do so, "schools should be the last to close and the first to re-open," Vaillancourt said.

She believes initiatives to address pandemic learning loss are required across K-12 into post-secondary and will be for years to come.

We can't think "that because the pandemic feels like it was so long ago, that there's nothing to be done, that the ship has sailed," she said.

"Even though this was in the past, we still have these learners in our system — they're still in my system at the university level — and they still need help."

title: Nicht jede Prüfung ist bedroht – Warum der Veränderungsdruck durch KI ungleich verteilt ist
summary:
Dass sich Prüfungen durch generative KI verändern müssen, ist inzwischen Konsens. Im Prüfungsalltag hilft diese Diagnose aber wenig, denn sie behandelt alle Prüfungen gleich. Christian K. Karl von der Universität Duisburg-Essen schlägt vor, jede Prüfung an zwei Fragen zu messen: Was kann KI hier tun – und wie stark verändert das die Aussagekraft der Prüfung? Die Antworten fallen je nach Prüfungselement und Fachkultur sehr unterschiedlich aus.

The post Nicht jede Prüfung ist bedroht – Warum der Veränderungsdruck durch KI ungleich verteilt ist appeared first on Hochschulforum Digitalisierung.
full_text:
Dass sich Prüfungen durch generative KI verändern müssen, ist inzwischen Konsens. Im Prüfungsalltag hilft diese Diagnose aber wenig, denn sie behandelt alle Prüfungen gleich. Christian K. Karl von der Universität Duisburg-Essen schlägt vor, jede Prüfung an zwei Fragen zu messen: Was kann KI hier tun – und wie stark verändert das die Aussagekraft der Prüfung? Die Antworten fallen je nach Prüfungselement und Fachkultur sehr unterschiedlich aus.

Kaum eine hochschuldidaktische Debatte hat so schnell einen Konsens gefunden wie die über KI und Prüfungen. Prüfungen müssen neu gedacht werden, heißt es, auch hier im Blog (Lenz-Kesekamp, 2026). Generelle KI-Verbote gelten als weder rechtlich noch praktisch sinnvoll (Schorer & Meier zu Farwig, 2025). Die Hochschulen haben reagiert, allerdings vor allem mit weichen Instrumenten: Nach dem KI-Monitor 2025 haben 87 Prozent ihre Eigenständigkeitserklärungen angepasst, aber nur 43 Prozent ihre Prüfungsordnungen. Eine verabschiedete KI-Strategie haben lediglich 15 Prozent.

Wer heute eine Modulprüfung plant, steht vor einer anderen Frage als die Debatte. Muss sich meine Prüfung ändern, und wenn ja, wie stark? Darauf gibt die Diagnose eines Wandels der Prüfungskultur keine Antwort. Sie spricht über „die Prüfung“, als gäbe es nur eine. Das ist aktuell ihr größter blinder Fleck.

Im Projekt KI4Edu, gefördert von der Stiftung Innovation in der Hochschullehre, haben wir an der Universität Duisburg-Essen ein kompetenzorientiertes Prüfungsmodell auf seine Tragfähigkeit unter KI-Bedingungen untersucht. Ausgangspunkt war das Prüfungsmodell LOCAM, das ich 2011 entwickelt habe. Es zerlegt eine Prüfung in ihre Bausteine: Organisation, Durchführung, Inhalte, Bewertungskriterien und Evaluation.

An jeden Baustein haben wir zwei Fragen gerichtet. Was kann KI hier tun? Das bestimmt den Unterstützungsnutzen. Wie stark verändert diese KI-Rolle die Logik des Prüfungsformats? Das bestimmt den Transformationsdruck. Aus beiden zusammen entsteht eine KI-sensitive Erweiterung des Modells, LOCAM-AI, mit drei Typen von Prüfungselementen (KI4Edu-Report Nr. 7). Der Befund mag unbequem für beide Lager der Debatte sein: Ein großer Teil des Prüfungswesens kann bleiben, wie er ist. Ein kleiner Teil muss dagegen grundlegend neu gebaut werden.

Prüfungsorganisation und Evaluation gewinnen durch KI, ohne dass ihre Logik kippt. KI kann Termine und Ressourcen planen, Rückmeldungen von Studierenden verdichten, Muster in Bewertungen sichtbar machen oder Aufgabenformulierungen auf Verständlichkeit prüfen. Hoher Nutzen, geringer Druck: Das ist Typ A. Die Grenze liegt genau dort, wo aus einer KI-Analyse eine Entscheidung wird. Die Deutung bleibt somit immer bei den Prüfenden.

Quer zu diesen Typen lohnt ein Blick auf die Formate, und auch dort gibt es Stabilität. Mündliche Prüfungen, Kolloquien, beaufsichtigte Prüfungen und praktische Demonstrationen bleiben aussagekräftig, weil Bearbeitungsweg und Person in ihnen unmittelbar sichtbar werden. Wo eigenständiges Wissen, manuelle Fertigkeiten oder sicherheitskritisches Urteilen nachzuweisen sind, ist der Ausschluss von KI weiterhin eine legitime Entscheidung – sofern er strukturell gesichert ist und nicht nur in der Aufgabenstellung steht.

Bei Prüfungsinhalten und Bewertungskriterien bietet KI erkennbaren Mehrwert, verschiebt aber die Maßstäbe. Reproduktive und standardisierte Aufgaben verlieren an Aussagekraft, Transfer, Kontextualisierung, Urteil und Reflexion werden damit umso wichtiger. Das Format kann hier bleiben, die Bewertung muss sich jedoch ändern. Eine reine Produktbewertung reicht nicht mehr, weil das Endprodukt nicht mehr zuverlässig zeigt, welche Kompetenz dahintersteht.

Orientierung dazu bietet das 3P-Modell aus dem HFD-Diskussionspapier zu Abschlussarbeiten (Weßels, Bils & Budde, 2025). Für Bewertungsraster heißt das konkret: Sie sollten das fachliche Ergebnis, den Bearbeitungsweg, die Qualität der Reflexion, den Umfang der KI-Unterstützung und den eigenen Beitrag getrennt ausweisen.

Den stärksten Druck trägt die Durchführung, und dort vor allem das unbeaufsichtigt erstellte schriftliche Endprodukt. Hausarbeit, Seminararbeit und Hausübung beruhen auf der Annahme, dass die vorgelegte Bearbeitung Ausdruck individueller Leistung ist. Diese Annahme trägt im KI-Zeitalter eben nicht mehr.

Daran ändern Deklarationspflichten und Erlaubnisstufen wenig. Corbin, Dawson und Liu (2025) unterscheiden diskursive Änderungen, die nur mitteilen, was erlaubt ist, von strukturellen Änderungen, welche die Mechanik der Aufgabe selbst verändern. Diskursive Regeln erzeugen nach ihrer Analyse eine „enforcement illusion“: Sie beschreiben Grenzen, die niemand überprüfen kann. Das heißt, Validität entsteht erst durch eine veränderte Aufgabe.

Das heißt aber ausdrücklich nicht, dass die Hausarbeit verschwinden muss. Eine schriftliche Ausarbeitung bleibt aussagekräftig, wenn sie ergänzt wird durch Prozessdokumentation, Reflexion und eine angemessen lange und strukturierte mündliche Vorstellung mit Diskussion. Ersetzt werden muss die Hausarbeit ohne sichtbaren Prozess, z. B. durch Portfolio, Verteidigung oder dokumentierte Fallanalyse.

Wie stark der Druck ist, hängt auch von der Fachkultur ab. In der Bauwirtschaft wird KI zunehmend in Planung, Bauprojektmanagement, Nachhaltigkeitsbewertung, Dokumentenanalyse und Betrieb eingesetzt (KI4Edu-Reports Nr. 9 und Nr. 10). Der sachkundige Umgang mit KI wird damit selbst Teil beruflicher Handlungskompetenz. Eine Prüfung, die KI pauschal ausschließt, prüft dann an der Berufspraxis vorbei – und das kann auch nicht unser Ziel sein.

Zugleich sind Entscheidungen im Bauwesen häufig sicherheits-, kosten- und haftungsrelevant. Explorative Studien im Projektverbund mit unserem Schwesterprojekt Lehrentwicklung – Künstliche Intelligenz (LKI) der Hochschule Ruhr West zeigen, dass Sprachmodelle bei definitorischen und konzeptionellen Fragen häufig richtig liegen, bei normativen Fachinhalten und detailgenauen Klassifikationen aber vermehrt Fehler erzeugen (KI4Edu-Report Nr. 4). Genau dort liegt der prüfungsdidaktische Hebel: Nicht die KI-Nutzung wird geprüft, sondern die Fähigkeit, KI-Ergebnisse fachlich zu prüfen.

Ein Beispiel ist die dokumentierte KI-gestützte Fallanalyse eines Bauprojekts. Studierende untersuchen Terminrisiken oder Datenprobleme in einem Gebäudeinformationsmodell mit KI-Unterstützung. Bewertet wird das Ergebnis, aber ebenso, wie sie die Datenbasis beurteilen, welche KI-Ausgaben sie übernehmen oder verwerfen und wie sie ihre Entscheidung begründen. Ein kurzes Verteidigungsgespräch oder eine Übertragung auf eine ähnliche Aufgabe zeigt, ob sie Problem und Ergebnis wirklich durchdrungen haben.

Ich vermute, dass dieser Befund über das Bauwesen hinaus trägt. Überall dort, wo KI zur Berufspraxis gehört und Fehler Folgen haben, sollte die kritische Prüfung von KI-Ergebnissen selbst Prüfungsgegenstand werden. Übertragbar ist dabei die Frage, nicht die Antwort: Welche Kompetenzen eigenständig und ohne KI gesichert bleiben müssen, kann nur jede Fachkultur für sich bestimmen.

Die oft gehörte Frage „Wurde KI genutzt?“ führt in eine Misstrauenslogik, die sich weder technisch noch rechtlich einlösen lässt. Ergiebiger ist die Frage, ob eine Prüfung noch belegt, was sie belegen soll. Nicht jede Prüfung muss sich deshalb ändern. Aber jede sollte diese Frage beantworten können.

Einen umfassenden Überblick zu dem Thema – von der Nutzungspraxis über Recht und Governance bis zum Prüfungsmodell LOCAM-AI – gibt es demnächst zusammengefasst in einem eigenen Band in der Reihe „Doing Higher Education“ bei Springer VS. Die Kernergebnisse aus KI4Edu sind bereits jetzt als Kurzberichte über die Projektwebseite frei zugänglich.

title: AI a scuola: pseudonimizzazione, dati personali e rischi per gli studenti

I cookie tecnici sono necessari al funzionamento del sito web perché abilitano funzioni per facilitare la navigazione dell’utente, che per esempio potrà accedere al proprio profilo senza dover eseguire ogni volta il login oppure potrà selezionare la lingua con cui desidera navigare il sito senza doverla impostare ogni volta.

COOKIE ANALITICI

I cookie analitici, che possono essere di prima o di terza parte, sono installati per collezionare informazioni sull’uso del sito web. In particolare, sono utili per analizzare statisticamente gli accessi o le visite al sito stesso e per consentire al titolare di migliorarne la struttura, le logiche di navigazione e i contenuti.

COOKIE DI PROFILAZIONE E SOCIAL PLUGIN

I cookie di profilazione e i social plugin, che possono essere di prima o di terza parte, servono a tracciare la navigazione dell’utente, analizzare il suo comportamento ai fini marketing e creare profili in merito ai suoi gusti, abitudini, scelte, etc. In questo modo è possibile ad esempio trasmettere messaggi pubblicitari mirati in relazione agli interessi dell’utente ed in linea con le preferenze da questi manifestate nella navigazione online.

title: AI a scuola, come costruire la tutela dei dati: cosa dice il Garante privacy
summary:
Il Garante privacy dà parere favorevole allo schema di decreto sull’IA nelle scuole e chiede al Ministero supporto agli istituti, criteri per i fornitori e assistenza. La protezione dei dati degli studenti diventa parte della responsabilità educativa

L'articolo AI a scuola, come costruire la tutela dei dati: cosa dice il Garante privacy proviene da Agenda Digitale.
full_text:
Portare l’intelligenza artificiale a scuola significa decidere chi sceglie gli strumenti, chi protegge i dati degli studenti e chi aiuta i docenti a usarli. Affidare queste decisioni ai singoli istituti, senza un sostegno comune, rischia di far dipendere la qualità delle tutele dalle competenze disponibili in ciascuna scuola. È su questa responsabilità pubblica dell’innovazione che si misura la portata delle indicazioni del Garante privacy.

Il parere favorevole n. 787 del 20 ottobre 2026 riguarda lo schema di decreto del Ministero dell’Istruzione e del Merito sull’impiego dell’IA a beneficio di studenti e docenti. Le osservazioni dell’Autorità delineano un compito che continua dopo il primo intervento, cioè accompagnare le scuole nella scelta e nell’uso di tecnologie in evoluzione: “La governance delle AI non è solo un tema urgente per aziende e pubbliche amministrazioni, ma riveste forma di inedita urgenza e complessità per tutte le formazioni sociali individuate e disciplinate dalla costituzione italiana, inclusa la scuola”, spiega l’avvocato Rocco Panetta, Chairman di Panetta Consulting Group.

IA a scuola, perché servono criteri comuni

Il Garante invita il Ministero a fornire un supporto adeguato agli istituti, anche attraverso futuri interventi di indirizzo e regolazione. La richiesta affronta una difficoltà concreta: per adottare un servizio occorre valutarne le garanzie e capire quali responsabilità comporti. Un orientamento nazionale può offrire una base condivisa a chi deve prendere queste decisioni.

Da qui l’indicazione di orientare le scuole tra le soluzioni disponibili sul mercato, anche definendo standard, requisiti e modelli per i fornitori. Un’offerta rivolta all’istruzione deve poter essere esaminata rispetto a criteri riconoscibili: altrimenti ogni istituto si troverebbe a ricostruire da solo le domande da porre alle aziende.

Le richieste del Garante al Ministero

AmbitoIndicazioneSupporto continuativoIndirizzo anche per i successivi sviluppi tecnologiciScelta dei fornitoriPossibili standard, requisiti e modelli comuniServizi-tipoRiferimenti da mettere a disposizione degli istitutiAssistenza dedicataAffiancamento anche nei rapporti con le aziende

Sintesi qualitativa delle osservazioni: servizi-tipo e assistenza sono possibilità da valutare. Fonte: Garante privacy, parere n. 787 del 20 ottobre 2026.

Servizi-tipo e assistenza nei rapporti con le aziende

Tra le possibilità indicate figura l’individuazione di servizi-tipo da mettere a disposizione degli istituti. Il loro valore sarebbe offrire un riferimento operativo per la selezione e l’impiego delle soluzioni. Il parere invita inoltre a valutare un servizio dedicato di assistenza, anche per affiancare le scuole nei rapporti con le imprese fornitrici.

Le due proposte rispondono a esigenze collegate. Un riferimento comune aiuta a scegliere; l’assistenza serve quando bisogna comprendere le condizioni del servizio e confrontarsi con chi lo eroga. È un modo per dare continuità all’indirizzo ministeriale, traducendolo in supporto alle decisioni quotidiane degli istituti.

Proteggere l’identità degli studenti nell’uso dell’IA

La scelta del fornitore incide anche su come vengono gestite le utenze. Lo schema è accompagnato da un allegato tecnico sulle misure organizzative e di sicurezza per la pseudonimizzazione e l’uso consapevole dei sistemi. La tutela entra così nella progettazione del servizio, prima che lo strumento diventi parte delle attività didattiche.

Identificativi separati e attenzione ai prompt

Nel modello descritto dal parere, i sistemi operano con identificativi pseudonimizzati; le informazioni che li collegano ai singoli studenti restano separate, sotto il controllo della scuola e accessibili ai soggetti autorizzati. La separazione tra identità e utenza limita l’esposizione dei dati identificativi nell’utilizzo del servizio.

Questa protezione richiede coerenza anche nelle richieste rivolte all’IA. Un’utenza pseudonimizzata perde parte della sua funzione protettiva se nel prompt si inseriscono informazioni che identificano lo studente. Le indicazioni ai docenti riguardano perciò anche la formulazione di prompt non identificativi e la sensibilizzazione degli alunni a un impiego critico e consapevole.

Perché la governance comincia dalle istituzioni

Il legame tra protezione dei dati e formazione spiega perché il parere abbia una portata che va oltre l’adozione di un applicativo. La scuola educa anche attraverso le condizioni nelle quali propone una tecnologia: quali informazioni si possono condividere, chi può accedervi, a chi chiedere aiuto. Rocco Panetta colloca questo passaggio nella responsabilità delle istituzioni: “Chiaramente questo è un primo punto di partenza, non dobbiamo illuderci che con un parere dell’autorità di controllo si esauriscano gli obblighi a cui il ministero dell’istruzione e le scuole tutte sono chiamate nel costruire consapevolezza nell’ educare i giovani all’uso responsabile della tecnologia. Questo è il primo tassello della governance universale delle AI senza il quale tutto può andare perduto”.

Dalle indicazioni alla consapevolezza in classe

Il richiamo di Panetta alla formazione trova un riscontro operativo nel rapporto tra misure tecniche e comportamento degli utenti. Per una classe, capire perché una richiesta debba evitare dati identificativi significa riconoscere un limite preciso alla condivisione delle informazioni. La consapevolezza si costruisce nell’uso, con spiegazioni collegate alle attività che studenti e docenti svolgono.
